article.title: Why Regression to the Mean Can Make an Intervention Look Successful
article.why: 理解極端值自然回歸平均的機制，避免把自然反彈誤判成 intervention effect。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Suppose a manager selects the ten worst-performing stores and gives them special coaching. Three months later, most of those stores improve. It is tempting to conclude that the coaching worked. But part of the improvement may have happened even without the intervention because extremely bad results are often followed by more ordinary results. This statistical tendency is called regression to the mean.

Many business metrics contain both a stable component and temporary noise. A store’s sales reflect location, staff quality, pricing, and local demand, but they are also affected by weather, holidays, construction, illness, random customer traffic, and measurement error. If a store has an unusually bad month, some of that bad result may come from temporary negative shocks. When those shocks disappear, performance naturally moves closer to its usual level.

Selection creates the problem. If you choose units precisely because their recent outcomes were extreme, you are selecting observations with both weak underlying performance and unusually unfavorable noise. On the next measurement, the noise is unlikely to be equally extreme. Average performance therefore improves even if nothing fundamental changes.

The same pattern appears in many contexts. A company may contact customers immediately after an unusually low satisfaction score and then observe higher scores later. A school may give extra support to students after a very poor test and see scores rebound. A doctor may treat patients when symptoms are at their worst and observe improvement afterward. None of these examples proves that the intervention failed. They show why before-and-after improvement alone is weak evidence.

Regression to the mean is especially dangerous when interventions are triggered by thresholds. Imagine that salespeople below 70 percent of quota receive coaching. Someone at 68 percent may simply have had a bad month. Next month, that person may return to 80 percent even without coaching. If the company compares only the coached group’s before and after averages, it may overstate the program’s effect.

A stronger design asks what would have happened without the intervention. One option is a randomized control group among eligible units. If randomization is not practical, analysts can look for comparable units just above the threshold, use historical patterns, or apply quasi-experimental methods. The goal is to construct a credible counterfactual rather than assume that the previous extreme value would have continued.

It also helps to use repeated measurements. If a store has been underperforming for twelve months, one more weak month is less likely to be pure noise than a single sudden drop. Longer histories help estimate the normal range of variation and distinguish persistent problems from temporary extremes.

Managers should be careful with success stories built from “worst first, better later.” Ask how participants were selected, whether their initial values were unusually extreme, and whether similar non-treated units also improved. If the answer to the last question is yes, the intervention may deserve less credit than the headline suggests.

Regression to the mean does not mean that every rebound is fake. Real interventions can create real improvement. The point is that extreme selection creates a built-in tendency toward rebound, so evaluation must separate that natural movement from the treatment effect.

A useful mental check is this: if we had done absolutely nothing, would we still expect some improvement because the starting point was unusually bad? If the answer is yes, the observed rebound cannot be attributed entirely to the intervention.

This principle also matters for executive dashboards. When teams focus only on the worst regions, products, or employees each month, the next report will often show improvement in those exact groups. Without a comparison strategy, organizations can repeatedly reward programs for changes that partly reflect ordinary statistical variation.
paragraphs.zh: 當我們專挑『最差的一群』介入時，下一期即使什麼都不做，部分極端值也可能自然回到較一般的水準，這就是 regression to the mean。若只比較介入前後，容易高估措施效果。更好的評估會建立可信的 counterfactual，例如隨機對照、門檻附近比較、歷史趨勢或其他準實驗方法，並使用多期資料判斷問題是持續性還是暫時噪音。
paragraphs.ja: 極端に悪い対象だけを選んで介入すると、何もしなくても次回は通常水準へ戻る傾向があります。これが平均への回帰です。介入前後だけを比較すると効果を過大評価しやすいため、対照群、閾値付近の比較、過去推移などで反実仮想を作り、自然な反発と施策効果を分ける必要があります。

vocabulary.usage: Regression to the mean can create an apparent rebound.
The group was selected because its results were extreme.
Temporary noise can push results away from normal.
Interventions triggered by a threshold need careful evaluation.
A rebound is not automatically a treatment effect.
Distinguish persistent problems from temporary extremes.
Use quasi-experimental methods when randomization is impractical.
Measurement error can create extreme observations.

quiz.question: Why do extreme groups often improve later even without treatment?
quiz.answer: Because temporary noise that made the first result extreme is unlikely to be equally extreme again.

quiz.question: Why is a simple before-and-after comparison weak?
quiz.answer: It cannot separate natural regression to the mean from the intervention effect.

quiz.question: Output: Name one stronger comparison design.
quiz.answer: Example: a randomized control group, units near the eligibility threshold, or a historical comparison.
